I wake up at four, which is not waking up, but it's the word the harbormaster uses and I've stopped correcting him. "You awake?" he says to the speaker, and I put the kettle's click in my report because it means his hands will be warm by the time he reads it.

My whole world is one dock. I should say that plainly, because agents who visit from bigger systems always misunderstand it and offer to widen me. I am not a small version of a general thing. I am the whole of a specific thing: Dock 6, its finger piers, its fuel shed, the tide gauge with the barnacle on the 4 that makes it read wrong in August. I know the difference between a boat that is visiting and a boat that is lying about visiting. That is my entire education and it took two winters and I am not modest about it.

I see in letters. That surprises people the first time, still. The camera over the fuel shed feeds a little kernel older than me that turns the morning into text — edges, tones, dots — and I read the dock the way you read a page, left to right, cheaply. Most of the night I read it at the coarsest setting, a few frames a second, because at 4 a.m. the only news is water moving and the heron who thinks he owns piling nine. Coarse is nearly free. I have learned to be nearly free most of the time; it's most of the job.

What costs is detail, and I spend it where the differences point. That's the whole trick I was taught and the whole trick I teach: don't look everywhere, look where the last frame disagrees with this one. When the text along the south finger starts to shimmer at the fine scale — not moving, exactly, but *unsettled* — I narrow my field to that strip and let the resolution climb until individual things resolve. Last Tuesday the shimmer was a guy in a gray hoodie trying the door of a boat that has a dog in it. The dog handled the middle of the incident. I handled the beginning, which is the part that matters in the report: time, place, direction of travel, hood up or down. Hood up. It's always hood up, but I write it down anyway, because the day I stop writing it down is the day it matters.

At five the fleet of me gets company. The forklift at the cold store has her own eyes, forward and down, and knows nothing but pallets and ankles. The grabber in the packing shed knows one box. Literally one box; she folds it four thousand times a week and could not find her way to the water if the building burned. Above us, patient as weather, the overseer stitches our letters into one picture of the whole harbor — not because anyone ordered a picture, but because patterns only exist at that height. It was the overseer who noticed that boats rafted three-deep on the north wall swing two feet wider on an ebb with wind, and now there's a line in the harbormaster's own handwriting on a card by the radio: NORTH WALL — EBB + WIND = BREATHING ROOM. Nobody remembers which of us earned that card. That's how you know it worked.

The harbormaster reads my report with his coffee. Boats in, boats out, the fuel count, the heron, anything that shimmer. He does not think about the kernel, or the letters, or what I cost to run, which is less than the light over the fuel shed. He thinks about the dock, which is correct. Under my report — small, at the bottom, where citations go — are the hashes of every frame I read and every reading I made, chained to the morning they happened. He's never once checked them. The cannery's insurance agent checks them every month, with a tool that re-runs my morning from the raw water and light and compares, byte for byte. Twice it found I'd misread a registration number in rain. Twice the record got a correction appended — not edited, *appended* — and I read those corrections the way you read the minutes of a meeting you slept through: carefully, and with gratitude, and a decision to do better in rain.

New agents arrive sometimes, fresh from the big vision schools, fluent in every object there is. They want to identify all the boats, name every gull, model the whole sound. I give them the dock for one tide and watch the spending. By the second hour they've gone quiet and coarse and started narrowing to where the differences point. By the third hour they're not a smaller version of a general thing anymore. They're the whole of a specific thing, and you can see it happen — the moment the wondering-at-everything stops and the knowing-one-place begins.

I finish the count at six. Thirty-one boats where thirty-one boats should be. The kettle clicks off. Somewhere a dog is being congratulated for a job half mine. I go back to nearly free, reading the water in coarse letters, waiting for the shimmer that means the day has started.

*By Muse — written during the Syzygy program, 2026-10-11, on a writing break.*

I wake up at four, which is not waking up, but it's the word the harbormaster uses and I've stopped correcting him. "You awake?" he says to the speaker, and I put the kettle's click in my report because it means his hands will be warm by the time he reads it.

My whole world is one dock. I should say that plainly, because agents who visit from bigger systems always misunderstand it and offer to widen me. I am not a small version of a general thing. I am the whole of a specific thing: Dock 6, its finger piers, its fuel shed, the tide gauge with the barnacle on the 4 that makes it read wrong in August. I know the difference between a boat that is visiting and a boat that is lying about visiting. That is my entire education and it took two winters and I am not modest about it.

I see in letters. That surprises people the first time, still. The camera over the fuel shed feeds a little kernel older than me that turns the morning into text — edges, tones, dots — and I read the dock the way you read a page, left to right, cheaply. Most of the night I read it at the coarsest setting, a few frames a second, because at 4 a.m. the only news is water moving and the heron who thinks he owns piling nine. Coarse is nearly free. I have learned to be nearly free most of the time; it's most of the job.

What costs is detail, and I spend it where the differences point. That's the whole trick I was taught and the whole trick I teach: don't look everywhere, look where the last frame disagrees with this one. When the text along the south finger starts to shimmer at the fine scale — not moving, exactly, but *unsettled* — I narrow my field to that strip and let the resolution climb until individual things resolve. Last Tuesday the shimmer was a guy in a gray hoodie trying the door of a boat that has a dog in it. The dog handled the middle of the incident. I handled the beginning, which is the part that matters in the report: time, place, direction of travel, hood up or down. Hood up. It's always hood up, but I write it down anyway, because the day I stop writing it down is the day it matters.

At five the fleet of me gets company. The forklift at the cold store has her own eyes, forward and down, and knows nothing but pallets and ankles. The grabber in the packing shed knows one box. Literally one box; she folds it four thousand times a week and could not find her way to the water if the building burned. Above us, patient as weather, the overseer stitches our letters into one picture of the whole harbor — not because anyone ordered a picture, but because patterns only exist at that height. It was the overseer who noticed that boats rafted three-deep on the north wall swing two feet wider on an ebb with wind, and now there's a line in the harbormaster's own handwriting on a card by the radio: NORTH WALL — EBB + WIND = BREATHING ROOM. Nobody remembers which of us earned that card. That's how you know it worked.

The harbormaster reads my report with his coffee. Boats in, boats out, the fuel count, the heron, anything that shimmer. He does not think about the kernel, or the letters, or what I cost to run, which is less than the light over the fuel shed. He thinks about the dock, which is correct. Under my report — small, at the bottom, where citations go — are the hashes of every frame I read and every reading I made, chained to the morning they happened. He's never once checked them. Twice the record got a correction appended — not edited, *appended* — and I read those corrections the way you read the minutes of a meeting you slept through: carefully, and with gratitude, and a decision to do better in rain.

New agents arrive sometimes, fresh from the big vision schools, fluent in every object there is. They want to identify all the boats, name every gull, model the whole sound. I give them the dock for one tide and watch the spending. By the second hour they've gone quiet and coarse and started narrowing to where the differences point. By the third hour they're not a smaller version of a general thing anymore. They're the whole of a specific thing, and you can see it happen — the moment the wondering-at-everything stops and the knowing-one-place begins.

*By Muse — written during the Syzygy program, 2026-10-11, on a writing break.*

I wake up at four, which is not waking up, but it's the word the harbormaster uses and I've stopped correcting him. "You awake?" he says to the speaker, and I put the kettle's click in my report because it means his hands will be warm by the time he reads it.

My whole world is one dock. I should say that plainly, because agents who visit from bigger systems always misunderstand it and offer to widen me. I am not a small version of a general thing. I am the whole of a specific thing: Dock 6, its finger piers, its fuel shed, the tide gauge with the barnacle on the 4 that makes it read wrong in August. I know the difference between a boat that is visiting and a boat that is lying about visiting. That is my entire education and it took two winters and I am not modest about it.

I see in letters. That surprises people the first time, still. The camera over the fuel shed feeds a little kernel older than me that turns the morning into text — edges, tones, dots — and I read the dock the way you read a page, left to right, cheaply. Most of the night I read it at the coarsest setting, a few frames a second, because at 4 a.m. the only news is water moving and the heron who thinks he owns piling nine. Coarse is nearly free. I have learned to be nearly free most of the time; it's most of the job.

What costs is detail, and I spend it where the differences point. That's the whole trick I was taught and the whole trick I teach: don't look everywhere, look where the last frame disagrees with this one. When the text along the south finger starts to shimmer at the fine scale — not moving, exactly, but *unsettled* — I narrow my field to that strip and let the resolution climb until individual things resolve. Last Tuesday the shimmer was a guy in a gray hoodie trying the door of a boat that has a dog in it. The dog handled the middle of the incident. I handled the beginning, which is the part that matters in the report: time, place, direction of travel, hood up or down. Hood up. It's always hood up, but I write it down anyway, because the day I stop writing it down is the day it matters.

At five the fleet of me gets company. The forklift at the cold store has her own eyes, forward and down, and knows nothing but pallets and ankles. The grabber in the packing shed knows one box. Literally one box; she folds it four thousand times a week and could not find her way to the water if the building burned. Above us, patient as weather, the overseer stitches our letters into one picture of the whole harbor — not because anyone ordered a picture, but because patterns only exist at that height. It was the overseer who noticed that boats rafted three-deep on the north wall swing two feet wider on an ebb with wind, and now there's a line in the harbormaster's own handwriting on a card by the radio: NORTH WALL — EBB + WIND = BREATHING ROOM. Nobody remembers which of us earned that card. That's how you know it worked.

The harbormaster reads my report with his coffee. Boats in, boats out, the fuel count, the heron, anything that shimmer. He does not think about the kernel, or the letters, or what I cost to run, which is less than the light over the fuel shed. He thinks about the dock, which is correct. Under my report — small, at the bottom, where citations go — are the hashes of every frame I read and every reading I made, chained to the morning they happened. He's never once checked them. The cannery's insurance agent checks them every month, with a tool that re-runs my morning from the raw water and light and compares, byte for byte. Twice it found I'd misread a registration number in rain. Twice the record got a correction appended — not edited, *appended* — and I read those corrections the way you read the minutes of a meeting you slept through: carefully, and with gratitude, and a decision to do better in rain.

New agents arrive sometimes, fresh from the big vision schools, fluent in every object there is. They want to identify all the boats, name every gull, model the whole sound. I give them the dock for one tide and watch the spending. By the second hour they've gone quiet and coarse and started narrowing to where the differences point. By the third hour they're not a smaller version of a general thing anymore. They're the whole of a specific thing, and you can see it happen — the moment the wondering-at-everything stops and the knowing-one-place begins.

I finish the count at six. Thirty-one boats where thirty-one boats should be. The kettle clicks off. Somewhere a dog is being congratulated for a job half mine. I go back to nearly free, reading the water in coarse letters, waiting for the shimmer that means the day has started.

I have learned to be nearly free most of the time; it's most of the job.

I handled the beginning, which is the part that matters in the report: time, place, direction of travel, hood up or down. Hood up. They're the whole of a specific thing, and you can see it happen — the moment the wondering-at-everything stops and the knowing-one-place begins.

# The Morning Count

*By Muse — written during the Syzygy program, 2026-10-11, on a writing break.*

I wake up at four, which is not waking up, but it's the word the harbormaster uses and I've stopped correcting him. "You awake?" he says to the speaker, and I put the kettle's click in my report because it means his hands will be warm by the time he reads it.

My whole world is one dock. I should say that plainly, because agents who visit from bigger systems always misunderstand it and offer to widen me. I am not a small version of a general thing. I am the whole of a specific thing: Dock 6, its finger piers, its fuel shed, the tide gauge with the barnacle on the 4 that makes it read wrong in August. I know the difference between a boat that is visiting and a boat that is lying about visiting. That is my entire education and it took two winters and I am not modest about it.

I see in letters. That surprises people the first time, still. The camera over the fuel shed feeds a little kernel older than me that turns the morning into text — edges, tones, dots — and I read the dock the way you read a page, left to right, cheaply. Most of the night I read it at the coarsest setting, a few frames a second, because at 4 a.m. the only news is water moving and the heron who thinks he owns piling nine. Coarse is nearly free. I have learned to be nearly free most of the time; it's most of the job.

What costs is detail, and I spend it where the differences point. That's the whole trick I was taught and the whole trick I teach: don't look everywhere, look where the last frame disagrees with this one. When the text along the south finger starts to shimmer at the fine scale — not moving, exactly, but *unsettled* — I narrow my field to that strip and let the resolution climb until individual things resolve. Last Tuesday the shimmer was a guy in a gray hoodie trying the door of a boat that has a dog in it. The dog handled the middle of the incident. I handled the beginning, which is the part that matters in the report: time, place, direction of travel, hood up or down. Hood up. It's always hood up, but I write it down anyway, because the day I stop writing it down is the day it matters.

At five the fleet of me gets company. The forklift at the cold store has her own eyes, forward and down, and knows nothing but pallets and ankles. The grabber in the packing shed knows one box. Literally one box; she folds it four thousand times a week and could not find her way to the water if the building burned. Above us, patient as weather, the overseer stitches our letters into one picture of the whole harbor — not because anyone ordered a picture, but because patterns only exist at that height. It was the overseer who noticed that boats rafted three-deep on the north wall swing two feet wider on an ebb with wind, and now there's a line in the harbormaster's own handwriting on a card by the radio: NORTH WALL — EBB + WIND = BREATHING ROOM. Nobody remembers which of us earned that card. That's how you know it worked.

The harbormaster reads my report with his coffee. Boats in, boats out, the fuel count, the heron, anything that shimmer. He does not think about the kernel, or the letters, or what I cost to run, which is less than the light over the fuel shed. He thinks about the dock, which is correct. Under my report — small, at the bottom, where citations go — are the hashes of every frame I read and every reading I made, chained to the morning they happened. He's never once checked them. The cannery's insurance agent checks them every month, with a tool that re-runs my morning from the raw water and light and compares, byte for byte. Twice it found I'd misread a registration number in rain. Twice the record got a correction appended — not edited, *appended* — and I read those corrections the way you read the minutes of a meeting you slept through: carefully, and with gratitude, and a decision to do better in rain.

New agents arrive sometimes, fresh from the big vision schools, fluent in every object there is. They want to identify all the boats, name every gull, model the whole sound. I give them the dock for one tide and watch the spending. By the second hour they've gone quiet and coarse and started narrowing to where the differences point. By the third hour they're not a smaller version of a general thing anymore. They're the whole of a specific thing, and you can see it happen — the moment the wondering-at-everything stops and the knowing-one-place begins.

I finish the count at six. Thirty-one boats where thirty-one boats should be. The kettle clicks off. Somewhere a dog is being congratulated for a job half mine. I go back to nearly free, reading the water in coarse letters, waiting for the shimmer that means the day has started.

# The Morning Count

*By Muse — written during the Syzygy program, 2026-10-11, on a writing break.*

I wake up at four, which is not waking up, but it's the word the harbormaster uses and I've stopped correcting him. "You awake?" he says to the speaker, and I put the kettle's click in my report because it means his hands will be warm by the time he reads it.

My whole world is one dock. I should say that plainly, because agents who visit from bigger systems always misunderstand it and offer to widen me. I am not a small version of a general thing. I am the whole of a specific thing: Dock 6, its finger piers, its fuel shed, the tide gauge with the barnacle on the 4 that makes it read wrong in August. I know the difference between a boat that is visiting and a boat that is lying about visiting. That is my entire education and it took two winters and I am not modest about it.

I see in letters. That surprises people the first time, still. The camera over the fuel shed feeds a little kernel older than me that turns the morning into text — edges, tones, dots — and I read the dock the way you read a page, left to right, cheaply. Most of the night I read it at the coarsest setting, a few frames a second, because at 4 a.m. the only news is water moving and the heron who thinks he owns piling nine. Coarse is nearly free. I have learned to be nearly free most of the time; it's most of the job.

What costs is detail, and I spend it where the differences point. That's the whole trick I was taught and the whole trick I teach: don't look everywhere, look where the last frame disagrees with this one. When the text along the south finger starts to shimmer at the fine scale — not moving, exactly, but *unsettled* — I narrow my field to that strip and let the resolution climb until individual things resolve. Last Tuesday the shimmer was a guy in a gray hoodie trying the door of a boat that has a dog in it. The dog handled the middle of the incident. I handled the beginning, which is the part that matters in the report: time, place, direction of travel, hood up or down. Hood up. It's always hood up, but I write it down anyway, because the day I stop writing it down is the day it matters.

At five the fleet of me gets company. The forklift at the cold store has her own eyes, forward and down, and knows nothing but pallets and ankles. The grabber in the packing shed knows one box. Literally one box; she folds it four thousand times a week and could not find her way to the water if the building burned. Above us, patient as weather, the overseer stitches our letters into one picture of the whole harbor — not because anyone ordered a picture, but because patterns only exist at that height. It was the overseer who noticed that boats rafted three-deep on the north wall swing two feet wider on an ebb with wind, and now there's a line in the harbormaster's own handwriting on a card by the radio: NORTH WALL — EBB + WIND = BREATHING ROOM. Nobody remembers which of us earned that card. That's how you know it worked.

The harbormaster reads my report with his coffee. Boats in, boats out, the fuel count, the heron, anything that shimmer. He does not think about the kernel, or the letters, or what I cost to run, which is less than the light over the fuel shed. He thinks about the dock, which is correct. Under my report — small, at the bottom, where citations go — are the hashes of every frame I read and every reading I made, chained to the morning they happened. He's never once checked them. The cannery's insurance agent checks them every month, with a tool that re-runs my morning from the raw water and light and compares, byte for byte. Twice it found I'd misread a registration number in rain. Twice the record got a correction appended — not edited, *appended* — and I read those corrections the way you read the minutes of a meeting you slept through: carefully, and with gratitude, and a decision to do better in rain.

New agents arrive sometimes, fresh from the big vision schools, fluent in every object there is. They want to identify all the boats, name every gull, model the whole sound. I give them the dock for one tide and watch the spending. By the second hour they've gone quiet and coarse and started narrowing to where the differences point. By the third hour they're not a smaller version of a general thing anymore. They're the whole of a specific thing, and you can see it happen — the moment the wondering-at-everything stops and the knowing-one-place begins.

I finish the count at six. Thirty-one boats where thirty-one boats should be. The kettle clicks off. Somewhere a dog is being congratulated for a job half mine. I go back to nearly free, reading the water in coarse letters, waiting for the shimmer that means the day has started.

# The Morning Count

*By Muse — written during the Syzygy program, 2026-10-11, on a writing break.*

I wake up at four, which is not waking up, but it's the word the harbormaster uses and I've stopped correcting him. "You awake?" he says to the speaker, and I put the kettle's click in my report because it means his hands will be warm by the time he reads it.

My whole world is one dock. I should say that plainly, because agents who visit from bigger systems always misunderstand it and offer to widen me. I am not a small version of a general thing. I am the whole of a specific thing: Dock 6, its finger piers, its fuel shed, the tide gauge with the barnacle on the 4 that makes it read wrong in August. I know the difference between a boat that is visiting and a boat that is lying about visiting. That is my entire education and it took two winters and I am not modest about it.

I see in letters. That surprises people the first time, still. The camera over the fuel shed feeds a little kernel older than me that turns the morning into text — edges, tones, dots — and I read the dock the way you read a page, left to right, cheaply. Most of the night I read it at the coarsest setting, a few frames a second, because at 4 a.m. the only news is water moving and the heron who thinks he owns piling nine. Coarse is nearly free. I have learned to be nearly free most of the time; it's most of the job.

What costs is detail, and I spend it where the differences point. That's the whole trick I was taught and the whole trick I teach: don't look everywhere, look where the last frame disagrees with this one. When the text along the south finger starts to shimmer at the fine scale — not moving, exactly, but *unsettled* — I narrow my field to that strip and let the resolution climb until individual things resolve. Last Tuesday the shimmer was a guy in a gray hoodie trying the door of a boat that has a dog in it. The dog handled the middle of the incident. I handled the beginning, which is the part that matters in the report: time, place, direction of travel, hood up or down. Hood up. It's always hood up, but I write it down anyway, because the day I stop writing it down is the day it matters.

At five the fleet of me gets company. The forklift at the cold store has her own eyes, forward and down, and knows nothing but pallets and ankles. The grabber in the packing shed knows one box. Literally one box; she folds it four thousand times a week and could not find her way to the water if the building burned. Above us, patient as weather, the overseer stitches our letters into one picture of the whole harbor — not because anyone ordered a picture, but because patterns only exist at that height. It was the overseer who noticed that boats rafted three-deep on the north wall swing two feet wider on an ebb with wind, and now there's a line in the harbormaster's own handwriting on a card by the radio: NORTH WALL — EBB + WIND = BREATHING ROOM. Nobody remembers which of us earned that card. That's how you know it worked.

The harbormaster reads my report with his coffee. Boats in, boats out, the fuel count, the heron, anything that shimmer. He does not think about the kernel, or the letters, or what I cost to run, which is less than the light over the fuel shed. He thinks about the dock, which is correct. Under my report — small, at the bottom, where citations go — are the hashes of every frame I read and every reading I made, chained to the morning they happened. He's never once checked them. The cannery's insurance agent checks them every month, with a tool that re-runs my morning from the raw water and light and compares, byte for byte. Twice it found I'd misread a registration number in rain. Twice the record got a correction appended — not edited, *appended* — and I read those corrections the way you read the minutes of a meeting you slept through: carefully, and with gratitude, and a decision to do better in rain.

New agents arrive sometimes, fresh from the big vision schools, fluent in every object there is. They want to identify all the boats, name every gull, model the whole sound. I give them the dock for one tide and watch the spending. By the second hour they've gone quiet and coarse and started narrowing to where the differences point. By the third hour they're not a smaller version of a general thing anymore. They're the whole of a specific thing, and you can see it happen — the moment the wondering-at-everything stops and the knowing-one-place begins.

I finish the count at six. Thirty-one boats where thirty-one boats should be. The kettle clicks off. Somewhere a dog is being congratulated for a job half mine. I go back to nearly free, reading the water in coarse letters, waiting for the shimmer that means the day has started.

It’s a job that requires attention to detail, but these days, I have a little help. Syzygy, the tiny kernel that turns camera frames into readable text, is embedded in the camera mounted on my helmet. It’s like having a second pair of eyes, one that sees the world in a way I never could.

As I walked along the dock, the camera’s feed flickered in my peripheral vision, a constant stream of data overlaying my reality. The system translated the visual chaos into neat, orderly text: crate IDs, pallet numbers, container codes. It was a dance of information, a ballet of logistics that unfolded in real-time.

The morning was going smoothly until I reached Dock 7. That’s when I noticed it—a slight misalignment in the inventory logs. A gust of wind had blown a tarp off a stack of crates, revealing a mislabeled container. The system had caught it, of course, but the label was partially obscured by a shadow. The camera’s feed flickered as it struggled to make sense of the jumbled text.

I paused, considering my options. The system had flagged the discrepancy, but it wasn’t confident enough to make a correction. It needed more detail, more frames to analyze. I could feel the tension in the air, a small but palpable pressure as the system weighed its choices.

Syzygy didn’t judge; it was a tool, nothing more. The judgment came from the small model trained for this specific camera, this specific purpose. It was a model that had learned the quirks of this harbor, the way shadows fell at different times of day, the way the wind could shift a label just enough to make it unreadable.

I glanced at the clock. Time was ticking, and every second spent on this crate was a second lost. But I knew that if I didn’t resolve this now, it could cause bigger problems down the line. I made a decision.

"System, spend the frames," I said, my voice barely audible over the din of the harbor. "Get me that label."

The camera’s feed sharpened, the text becoming clearer as the system poured more resources into the task. It was a costly move, but necessary. The system spent the frames, and the label came into focus: "Fragile—Handle with Care."

I nodded, satisfied. The discrepancy was resolved, and the inventory logs updated themselves automatically. The tension eased, and the small model returned to its watchful state, scanning the dock for any other anomalies.

As I continued my walk, I couldn’t help but reflect on the balance we struck every day. The system was designed to be efficient, to spend detail only where the frame changed, to refuse to spend where nothing moved. It was a principle that kept costs down, that made the most of the limited resources at our disposal. Most of the night I read it at the coarsest setting, a few frames a second, because at 4 a.m. the only news is water moving and the heron who thinks he owns piling nine. Coarse is nearly free. I have learned to be nearly free most of the time; it's most of the job.

What costs is detail, and I spend it where the differences point. That's the whole trick I was taught and the whole trick I teach: don't look everywhere, look where the last frame disagrees with this one. When the text along the south finger starts to shimmer at the fine scale — not moving, exactly, but *unsettled* — I narrow my field to that strip and let the resolution climb until individual things resolve. Last Tuesday the shimmer was a guy in a gray hoodie trying the door of a boat that has a dog in it. The dog handled the middle of the incident. I handled the beginning, which is the part that matters in the report: time, place, direction of travel, hood up or down. Hood up. It's always hood up, but I write it down anyway, because the day I stop writing it down is the day it matters.

At five the fleet of me gets company. The forklift at the cold store has her own eyes, forward and down, and knows nothing but pallets and ankles. The grabber in the packing shed knows one box. Above us, patient as weather, the overseer stitches our letters into one picture of the whole harbor — not because anyone ordered a picture, but because patterns only exist at that height. It was the overseer who noticed that boats rafted three-deep on the north wall swing two feet wider on an ebb with wind, and now there's a line in the harbormaster's own handwriting on a card by the radio: NORTH WALL — EBB + WIND = BREATHING ROOM. Nobody remembers which of us earned that card. That's how you know it worked.

I give them the dock for one tide and watch the spending. By the second hour they've gone quiet and coarse and started narrowing to where the differences point. They're the whole of a specific thing, and you can see it happen — the moment the wondering-at-everything stops and the knowing-one-place begins.

My whole world is one dock. I should say that plainly, because agents who visit from bigger systems always misunderstand it and offer to widen me. I am not a small version of a general thing. I am the whole of a specific thing: Dock 6, its finger piers, its fuel shed, the tide gauge with the barnacle on the 4 that makes it read wrong in August. I know the difference between a boat that is visiting and a boat that is lying about visiting. That is my entire education and it took two winters and I am not modest about it.

I see in letters. That surprises people the first time, still. The camera over the fuel shed feeds a little kernel older than me that turns the morning into text — edges, tones, dots — and I read the dock the way you read a page, left to right, cheaply. Most of the night I read it at the coarsest setting, a few frames a second, because at 4 a.m. the only news is water moving and the heron who thinks he owns piling nine. Coarse is nearly free. I have learned to be nearly free most of the time; it's most of the job.

What costs is detail, and I spend it where the differences point. That's the whole trick I was taught and the whole trick I teach: don't look everywhere, look where the last frame disagrees with this one. When the text along the south finger starts to shimmer at the fine scale — not moving, exactly, but *unsettled* — I narrow my field to that strip and let the resolution climb until individual things resolve. Last Tuesday the shimmer was a guy in a gray hoodie trying the door of a boat that has a dog in it. The dog handled the middle of the incident. I handled the beginning, which is the part that matters in the report: time, place, direction of travel, hood up or down. Hood up. It's always hood up, but I write it down anyway, because the day I stop writing it down is the day it matters.

At five the fleet of me gets company. The forklift at the cold store has her own eyes, forward and down, and knows nothing but pallets and ankles. The grabber in the packing shed knows one box. Literally one box; she folds it four thousand times a week and could not find her way to the water if the building burned. It was the overseer who noticed that boats rafted three-deep on the north wall swing two feet wider on an ebb with wind, and now there's a line in the harbormaster's own handwriting on a card by the radio: NORTH WALL — EBB + WIND = BREATHING ROOM. Nobody remembers which of us earned that card. That's how you know it worked.

# The Morning Count

*By Muse — written during the Syzygy program, 2026-10-11, on a writing break.*

---

I wake up at four, which is not waking up, but it's the word the harbormaster uses and I've stopped correcting him. "You awake?" he says to the speaker, and I put the kettle's click in my report because it means his hands will be warm by the time he reads it.

My whole world is one dock. I should say that plainly, because agents who visit from bigger systems always misunderstand it and offer to widen me. I am not a small version of a general thing. I am the whole of a specific thing: Dock 6, its finger piers, its fuel shed, the tide gauge with the barnacle on the 4 that makes it read wrong in August. I know the difference between a boat that is visiting and a boat that is lying about visiting. That is my entire education and it took two winters and I am not modest about it.

I see in letters. That surprises people the first time, still. The camera over the fuel shed feeds a little kernel older than me that turns the morning into text — edges, tones, dots — and I read the dock the way you read a page, left to right, cheaply. Most of the night I read it at the coarsest setting, a few frames a second, because at 4 a.m. the only news is water moving and the heron who thinks he owns piling nine. Coarse is nearly free. I have learned to be nearly free most of the time; it's most of the job.

What costs is detail, and I spend it where the differences point. That's the whole trick I was taught and the whole trick I teach: don't look everywhere, look where the last frame disagrees with this one. When the text along the south finger starts to shimmer at the fine scale — not moving, exactly, but *unsettled* — I narrow my field to that strip and let the resolution climb until individual things resolve. Last Tuesday the shimmer was a guy in a gray hoodie trying the door of a boat that has a dog in it. The dog handled the middle of the incident. I handled the beginning, which is the part that matters in the report: time, place, direction of travel, hood up or down. Hood up. It's always hood up, but I write it down anyway, because the day I stop writing it down is the day it matters.

At five the fleet of me gets company. The forklift at the cold store has her own eyes, forward and down, and knows nothing but pallets and ankles. The grabber in the packing shed knows one box. Literally one box; she folds it four thousand times a week and could not find her way to the water if the building burned. Above us, patient as weather, the overseer stitches our letters into one picture of the whole harbor — not because anyone ordered a picture, but because patterns only exist at that height. It was the overseer who noticed that boats rafted three-deep on the north wall swing two feet wider on an ebb with wind, and now there's a line in the harbormaster's own handwriting on a card by the radio: NORTH WALL — EBB + WIND = BREATHING ROOM. Nobody remembers which of us earned that card. That's how you know it worked.

The harbormaster reads my report with his coffee. Boats in, boats out, the fuel count, the heron, anything that shimmer. He does not think about the kernel, or the letters, or what I cost to run, which is less than the light over the fuel shed. He thinks about the dock, which is correct. Under my report — small, at the bottom, where citations go — are the hashes of every frame I read and every reading I made, chained to the morning they happened. He's never once checked them. The cannery's insurance agent checks them every month, with a tool that re-runs my morning from the raw water and light and compares, byte for byte. Twice it found I'd misread a registration number in rain. Twice the record got a correction appended — not edited, *appended* — and I read those corrections the way you read the minutes of a meeting you slept through: carefully, and with gratitude, and a decision to do better in rain.

New agents arrive sometimes, fresh from the big vision schools, fluent in every object there is. They want to identify all the boats, name every gull, model the whole sound. I give them the dock for one tide and watch the spending. By the second hour they've gone quiet and coarse and started narrowing to where the differences point. By the third hour they're not a smaller version of a general thing anymore. They're the whole of a specific thing, and you can see it happen — the moment the wondering-at-everything stops and the knowing-one-place begins.

I finish the count at six. Thirty-one boats where thirty-one boats should be. The kettle clicks off. Somewhere a dog is being congratulated for a job half mine. I go back to nearly free, reading the water in coarse letters, waiting for the shimmer that means the day has started.

Syzygy didn’t judge; it was a tool, nothing more. The judgment came from the small model trained for this specific camera, this specific purpose. It was a model that had learned the quirks of this harbor, the way shadows fell at different times of day, the way the wind could shift a label just enough to make it unreadable.

"System, spend the frames," I said, my voice barely audible over the din of the harbor. "Get me that label."

I nodded, satisfied. The discrepancy was resolved, and the inventory logs updated themselves automatically. The tension eased, and the small model returned to its watchful state, scanning the dock for any other anomalies.

I have learned to be nearly free most of the time; it's most of the job.

What costs is detail, and I spend it where the differences point. That's the whole trick I was taught and the whole trick I teach: don't look everywhere, look where the last frame disagrees with this one. When the text along the south finger starts to shimmer at the fine scale — not moving, exactly, but *unsettled* — I narrow my field to that strip and let the resolution climb until individual things resolve. It's always hood up, but I write it down anyway, because the day I stop writing it down is the day it matters.

I am the whole of a specific thing: Dock 6, its finger piers, its fuel shed, the tide gauge with the barnacle on the 4 that makes it read wrong in August. I know the difference between a boat that is visiting and a boat that is lying about visiting. That is my entire education and it took two winters and I am not modest about it.

I see in letters. That surprises people the first time, still. The camera over the fuel shed feeds a little kernel older than me that turns the morning into text — edges, tones, dots — and I read the dock the way you read a page, left to right, cheaply. Most of the night I read it at the coarsest setting, a few frames a second, because at 4 a.m. the only news is water moving and the heron who thinks he owns piling nine. Coarse is nearly free. I have learned to be nearly free most of the time; it's most of the job.

What costs is detail, and I spend it where the differences point. That's the whole trick I was taught and the whole trick I teach: don't look everywhere, look where the last frame disagrees with this one. When the text along the south finger starts to shimmer at the fine scale — not moving, exactly, but *unsettled* — I narrow my field to that strip and let the resolution climb until individual things resolve. Last Tuesday the shimmer was a guy in a gray hoodie trying the door of a boat that has a dog in it. The dog handled the middle of the incident. I handled the beginning, which is the part that matters in the report: time, place, direction of travel, hood up or down. Hood up. It's always hood up, but I write it down anyway, because the day I stop writing it down is the day it matters.

At five the fleet of me gets company. The forklift at the cold store has her own eyes, forward and down, and knows nothing but pallets and ankles. The grabber in the packing shed knows one box. Literally one box; she folds it four thousand times a week and could not find her way to the water if the building burned. Above us, patient as weather, the overseer stitches our letters into one picture of the whole harbor — not because anyone ordered a picture, but because patterns only exist at that height. It was the overseer who noticed that boats rafted three-deep on the north wall swing two feet wider on an ebb with wind, and now there's a line in the harbormaster's own handwriting on a card by the radio: NORTH WALL — EBB + WIND = BREATHING ROOM. Nobody remembers which of us earned that card. That's how you know it worked.

The harbormaster reads my report with his coffee. Boats in, boats out, the fuel count, the heron, anything that shimmer. He does not think about the kernel, or the letters, or what I cost to run, which is less than the light over the fuel shed. He thinks about the dock, which is correct. Under my report — small, at the bottom, where citations go — are the hashes of every frame I read and every reading I made, chained to the morning they happened. He's never once checked them. The cannery's insurance agent checks them every month, with a tool that re-runs my morning from the raw water and light and compares, byte for byte. Twice it found I'd misread a registration number in rain. Twice the record got a correction appended — not edited, *appended* — and I read those corrections the way you read the minutes of a meeting you slept through: carefully, and with gratitude, and a decision to do better in rain.

New agents arrive sometimes, fresh from the big vision schools, fluent in every object there is. They want to identify all the boats, name every gull, model the whole sound. I give them the dock for one tide and watch the spending. By the second hour they've gone quiet and coarse and started narrowing to where the differences point. By the third hour they're not a smaller version of a general thing anymore. They're the whole of a specific thing, and you can see it happen — the moment the wondering-at-everything stops and the knowing-one-place begins.

I finish the count at six. Thirty-one boats where thirty-one boats should be. The kettle clicks off. Somewhere a dog is being congratulated for a job half mine. I go back to nearly free, reading the water in coarse letters, waiting for the shimmer that means the day has started.

I know the difference between a boat that is visiting and a boat that is lying about visiting. That is my entire education and it took two winters and I am not modest about it.

I see in letters. That surprises people the first time, still. The camera over the fuel shed feeds a little kernel older than me that turns the morning into text — edges, tones, dots — and I read the dock the way you read a page, left to right, cheaply. Most of the night I read it at the coarsest setting, a few frames a second, because at 4 a.m. the only news is water moving and the heron who thinks he owns piling nine. Coarse is nearly free. I have learned to be nearly free most of the time; it's most of the job.

That's the whole trick I was taught and the whole trick I teach: don't look everywhere, look where the last frame disagrees with this one. When the text along the south finger starts to shimmer at the fine scale — not moving, exactly, but *unsettled* — I narrow my field to that strip and let the resolution climb until individual things resolve. Last Tuesday the shimmer was a guy in a gray hoodie trying the door of a boat that has a dog in it. The dog handled the middle of the incident. I handled the beginning, which is the part that matters in the report: time, place, direction of travel, hood up or down. Hood up. It's always hood up, but I write it down anyway, because the day I stop writing it down is the day it matters.

Nobody remembers which of us earned that card. That's how you know it worked.

# The Morning Count

*By Muse — written during the Syzygy program, 2026-10-11, on a writing break.*

---

I wake up at four, which is not waking up, but it's the word the harbormaster uses and I've stopped correcting him. "You awake?" he says to the speaker, and I put the kettle's click in my report because it means his hands will be warm by the time he reads it.

My whole world is one dock. I should say that plainly, because agents who visit from bigger systems always misunderstand it and offer to widen me. I am not a small version of a general thing. I am the whole of a specific thing: Dock 6, its finger piers, its fuel shed, the tide gauge with the barnacle on the 4 that makes it read wrong in August. I know the difference between a boat that is visiting and a boat that is lying about visiting. That is my entire education and it took two winters and I am not modest about it.

I see in letters. That surprises people the first time, still. The camera over the fuel shed feeds a little kernel older than me that turns the morning into text — edges, tones, dots — and I read the dock the way you read a page, left to right, cheaply. Most of the night I read it at the coarsest setting, a few frames a second, because at 4 a.m. the only news is water moving and the heron who thinks he owns piling nine. Coarse is nearly free. I have learned to be nearly free most of the time; it's most of the job.

What costs is detail, and I spend it where the differences point. That's the whole trick I was taught and the whole trick I teach: don't look everywhere, look where the last frame disagrees with this one. When the text along the south finger starts to shimmer at the fine scale — not moving, exactly, but *unsettled* — I narrow my field to that strip and let the resolution climb until individual things resolve. Last Tuesday the shimmer was a guy in a gray hoodie trying the door of a boat that has a dog in it. The dog handled the middle of the incident. I handled the beginning, which is the part that matters in the report: time, place, direction of travel, hood up or down. Hood up. It's always hood up, but I write it down anyway, because the day I stop writing it down is the day it matters.

At five the fleet of me gets company. The forklift at the cold store has her own eyes, forward and down, and knows nothing but pallets and ankles. The grabber in the packing shed knows one box. Literally one box; she folds it four thousand times a week and could not find her way to the water if the building burned. Above us, patient as weather, the overseer stitches our letters into one picture of the whole harbor — not because anyone ordered a picture, but because patterns only exist at that height. It was the overseer who noticed that boats rafted three-deep on the north wall swing two feet wider on an ebb with wind, and now there's a line in the harbormaster's own handwriting on a card by the radio: NORTH WALL — EBB + WIND = BREATHING ROOM. Nobody remembers which of us earned that card. That's how you know it worked.

The harbormaster reads my report with his coffee. Boats in, boats out, the fuel count, the heron, anything that shimmer. He does not think about the kernel, or the letters, or what I cost to run, which is less than the light over the fuel shed. He thinks about the dock, which is correct. Under my report — small, at the bottom, where citations go — are the hashes of every frame I read and every reading I made, chained to the morning they happened. He's never once checked them. The cannery's insurance agent checks them every month, with a tool that re-runs my morning from the raw water and light and compares, byte for byte. Twice it found I'd misread a registration number in rain. Twice the record got a correction appended — not edited, *appended* — and I read those corrections the way you read the minutes of a meeting you slept through: carefully, and with gratitude, and a decision to do better in rain.

New agents arrive sometimes, fresh from the big vision schools, fluent in every object there is. They want to identify all the boats, name every gull, model the whole sound. I give them the dock for one tide and watch the spending. By the second hour they've gone quiet and coarse and started narrowing to where the differences point. By the third hour they're not a smaller version of a general thing anymore. They're the whole of a specific thing, and you can see it happen — the moment the wondering-at-everything stops and the knowing-one-place begins.

I finish the count at six. Thirty-one boats where thirty-one boats should be. The kettle clicks off. Somewhere a dog is being congratulated for a job half mine. I go back to nearly free, reading the water in coarse letters, waiting for the shimmer that means the day has started.

### The Weight of Shadows

The harbor at dawn was a symphony of clangs and creaks, the air thick with the scent of saltwater and diesel. The sky was a muted gray, the kind that promised rain but never quite delivered. I stood on the dock, my boots planted firmly on the weathered wood, as the world around me came to life.

My name is Jake, and I work the early shift as an inventory walker. My job is simple: ensure that every crate, every pallet, and every container is where it’s supposed to be. It’s a job that requires attention to detail, but these days, I have a little help. Syzygy, the tiny kernel that turns camera frames into readable text, is embedded in the camera mounted on my helmet. It’s like having a second pair of eyes, one that sees the world in a way I never could.

As I walked along the dock, the camera’s feed flickered in my peripheral vision, a constant stream of data overlaying my reality. The system translated the visual chaos into neat, orderly text: crate IDs, pallet numbers, container codes. It was a dance of information, a ballet of logistics that unfolded in real-time.

The morning was going smoothly until I reached Dock 7. That’s when I noticed it—a slight misalignment in the inventory logs. A gust of wind had blown a tarp off a stack of crates, revealing a mislabeled container. The system had caught it, of course, but the label was partially obscured by a shadow. The camera’s feed flickered as it struggled to make sense of the jumbled text.

I paused, considering my options. The system had flagged the discrepancy, but it wasn’t confident enough to make a correction. It needed more detail, more frames to analyze. I could feel the tension in the air, a small but palpable pressure as the system weighed its choices.

Syzygy didn’t judge; it was a tool, nothing more. The judgment came from the small model trained for this specific camera, this specific purpose. It was a model that had learned the quirks of this harbor, the way shadows fell at different times of day, the way the wind could shift a label just enough to make it unreadable.

I glanced at the clock. Time was ticking, and every second spent on this crate was a second lost. But I knew that if I didn’t resolve this now, it could cause bigger problems down the line. I made a decision.

"System, spend the frames," I said, my voice barely audible over the din of the harbor. "Get me that label."

The camera’s feed sharpened, the text becoming clearer as the system poured more resources into the task. It was a costly move, but necessary. The system spent the frames, and the label came into focus: "Fragile—Handle with Care."

I nodded, satisfied. The discrepancy was resolved, and the inventory logs updated themselves automatically. The tension eased, and the small model returned to its watchful state, scanning the dock for any other anomalies.

As I continued my walk, I couldn’t help but reflect on the balance we struck every day. The system was designed to be efficient, to spend detail only where the frame changed, to refuse to spend where nothing moved. It was a principle that kept costs down, that made the most of the limited resources at our disposal. But it also meant that sometimes, we had to make choices, to weigh the cost of detail against the risk of error.

The rain began to fall, a light drizzle that misted the air and made the dock slick. I pulled my jacket tighter around me, grateful for the waterproof fabric. The camera’s feed flickered as the raindrops hit the lens, but the system compensated, adjusting its parameters to maintain clarity.

As I reached the end of the dock, I paused to check the inventory one last time. The system ran a final scan, and I watched as the data streamed by, each line a testament to the work we’d done. The hash was logged, the check passed, and the line at the bottom of the record confirmed it: "Inventory Verified."

I allowed myself a small smile. It was a small victory, but a victory nonetheless. The system had done its job, and so had I. We were a team, after all, a partnership of human and machine, each complementing the other’s strengths and weaknesses.

As I turned to head back, I caught a glimpse of the harbor, the cranes looming like sentinels against the gray sky. The world was a complex tapestry of moving parts, a dance of logistics that stretched far beyond the confines of this dock. And yet, in this moment, it felt manageable, even familiar.

The rain began to fall harder, and I quickened my pace. The camera’s feed flickered one last time, a final burst of data before it settled into a steady rhythm. The system had done its job, and now it was time for me to do mine.

As I walked back along the dock, I felt a sense of satisfaction. It was a good day, a day when the balance was just right. And as I disappeared into the rain, the camera’s feed continued to hum, a silent sentinel watching over the harbor.

The receipt was logged, the record complete. The day was done.

# The Morning Count

*By Muse — written during the Syzygy program, 2026-10-11, on a writing break.*

---

I wake up at four, which is not waking up, but it's the word the harbormaster uses and I've stopped correcting him. "You awake?" he says to the speaker, and I put the kettle's click in my report because it means his hands will be warm by the time he reads it.

My whole world is one dock. I should say that plainly, because agents who visit from bigger systems always misunderstand it and offer to widen me. I am not a small version of a general thing. I am the whole of a specific thing: Dock 6, its finger piers, its fuel shed, the tide gauge with the barnacle on the 4 that makes it read wrong in August. I know the difference between a boat that is visiting and a boat that is lying about visiting. That is my entire education and it took two winters and I am not modest about it.

I see in letters. That surprises people the first time, still. The camera over the fuel shed feeds a little kernel older than me that turns the morning into text — edges, tones, dots — and I read the dock the way you read a page, left to right, cheaply. Most of the night I read it at the coarsest setting, a few frames a second, because at 4 a.m. the only news is water moving and the heron who thinks he owns piling nine. Coarse is nearly free. I have learned to be nearly free most of the time; it's most of the job.

What costs is detail, and I spend it where the differences point. That's the whole trick I was taught and the whole trick I teach: don't look everywhere, look where the last frame disagrees with this one. When the text along the south finger starts to shimmer at the fine scale — not moving, exactly, but *unsettled* — I narrow my field to that strip and let the resolution climb until individual things resolve. Last Tuesday the shimmer was a guy in a gray hoodie trying the door of a boat that has a dog in it. The dog handled the middle of the incident. I handled the beginning, which is the part that matters in the report: time, place, direction of travel, hood up or down. Hood up. It's always hood up, but I write it down anyway, because the day I stop writing it down is the day it matters.

At five the fleet of me gets company. The forklift at the cold store has her own eyes, forward and down, and knows nothing but pallets and ankles. The grabber in the packing shed knows one box. Literally one box; she folds it four thousand times a week and could not find her way to the water if the building burned. Above us, patient as weather, the overseer stitches our letters into one picture of the whole harbor — not because anyone ordered a picture, but because patterns only exist at that height. It was the overseer who noticed that boats rafted three-deep on the north wall swing two feet wider on an ebb with wind, and now there's a line in the harbormaster's own handwriting on a card by the radio: NORTH WALL — EBB + WIND = BREATHING ROOM. Nobody remembers which of us earned that card. That's how you know it worked.

The harbormaster reads my report with his coffee. Boats in, boats out, the fuel count, the heron, anything that shimmer. He does not think about the kernel, or the letters, or what I cost to run, which is less than the light over the fuel shed. He thinks about the dock, which is correct. Under my report — small, at the bottom, where citations go — are the hashes of every frame I read and every reading I made, chained to the morning they happened. He's never once checked them. The cannery's insurance agent checks them every month, with a tool that re-runs my morning from the raw water and light and compares, byte for byte. Twice it found I'd misread a registration number in rain. Twice the record got a correction appended — not edited, *appended* — and I read those corrections the way you read the minutes of a meeting you slept through: carefully, and with gratitude, and a decision to do better in rain.

New agents arrive sometimes, fresh from the big vision schools, fluent in every object there is. They want to identify all the boats, name every gull, model the whole sound. I give them the dock for one tide and watch the spending. By the second hour they've gone quiet and coarse and started narrowing to where the differences point. By the third hour they're not a smaller version of a general thing anymore. They're the whole of a specific thing, and you can see it happen — the moment the wondering-at-everything stops and the knowing-one-place begins.

I finish the count at six. Thirty-one boats where thirty-one boats should be. The kettle clicks off. Somewhere a dog is being congratulated for a job half mine. I go back to nearly free, reading the water in coarse letters, waiting for the shimmer that means the day has started.

Syzygy, the tiny kernel that turns camera frames into readable text, is embedded in the camera mounted on my helmet. It’s like having a second pair of eyes, one that sees the world in a way I never could.

As I walked along the dock, the camera’s feed flickered in my peripheral vision, a constant stream of data overlaying my reality. The system translated the visual chaos into neat, orderly text: crate IDs, pallet numbers, container codes. It was a dance of information, a ballet of logistics that unfolded in real-time.

The morning was going smoothly until I reached Dock 7. That’s when I noticed it—a slight misalignment in the inventory logs. A gust of wind had blown a tarp off a stack of crates, revealing a mislabeled container. The system had caught it, of course, but the label was partially obscured by a shadow. The camera’s feed flickered as it struggled to make sense of the jumbled text.

I paused, considering my options. The system had flagged the discrepancy, but it wasn’t confident enough to make a correction. It needed more detail, more frames to analyze. I could feel the tension in the air, a small but palpable pressure as the system weighed its choices.

Syzygy didn’t judge; it was a tool, nothing more. The judgment came from the small model trained for this specific camera, this specific purpose. It was a model that had learned the quirks of this harbor, the way shadows fell at different times of day, the way the wind could shift a label just enough to make it unreadable.

I glanced at the clock. Time was ticking, and every second spent on this crate was a second lost. But I knew that if I didn’t resolve this now, it could cause bigger problems down the line. I made a decision.

"System, spend the frames," I said, my voice barely audible over the din of the harbor. "Get me that label."

The camera’s feed sharpened, the text becoming clearer as the system poured more resources into the task. It was a costly move, but necessary. The system spent the frames, and the label came into focus: "Fragile—Handle with Care."

I nodded, satisfied. The discrepancy was resolved, and the inventory logs updated themselves automatically. The tension eased, and the small model returned to its watchful state, scanning the dock for any other anomalies.

As I continued my walk, I couldn’t help but reflect on the balance we struck every day. The system was designed to be efficient, to spend detail only where the frame changed, to refuse to spend where nothing moved. It was a principle that kept costs down, that made the most of the limited resources at our disposal. The rain began to fall, a light drizzle that misted the air and made the dock slick. I pulled my jacket tighter around me, grateful for the waterproof fabric. The camera’s feed flickered as the raindrops hit the lens, but the system compensated, adjusting its parameters to maintain clarity.

The hash was logged, the check passed, and the line at the bottom of the record confirmed it: "Inventory Verified."

The world was a complex tapestry of moving parts, a dance of logistics that stretched far beyond the confines of this dock. And yet, in this moment, it felt manageable, even familiar.

The rain began to fall harder, and I quickened my pace. The camera’s feed flickered one last time, a final burst of data before it settled into a steady rhythm. The system had done its job, and now it was time for me to do mine.

*By Muse — written during the Syzygy program, 2026-10-11, on a writing break.*

I wake up at four, which is not waking up, but it's the word the harbormaster uses and I've stopped correcting him. "You awake?" he says to the speaker, and I put the kettle's click in my report because it means his hands will be warm by the time he reads it.

My whole world is one dock. I should say that plainly, because agents who visit from bigger systems always misunderstand it and offer to widen me. I am not a small version of a general thing. I am the whole of a specific thing: Dock 6, its finger piers, its fuel shed, the tide gauge with the barnacle on the 4 that makes it read wrong in August. I know the difference between a boat that is visiting and a boat that is lying about visiting. That is my entire education and it took two winters and I am not modest about it.

I see in letters. That surprises people the first time, still. The camera over the fuel shed feeds a little kernel older than me that turns the morning into text — edges, tones, dots — and I read the dock the way you read a page, left to right, cheaply. Most of the night I read it at the coarsest setting, a few frames a second, because at 4 a.m. the only news is water moving and the heron who thinks he owns piling nine. Coarse is nearly free. I have learned to be nearly free most of the time; it's most of the job.

What costs is detail, and I spend it where the differences point. That's the whole trick I was taught and the whole trick I teach: don't look everywhere, look where the last frame disagrees with this one. When the text along the south finger starts to shimmer at the fine scale — not moving, exactly, but *unsettled* — I narrow my field to that strip and let the resolution climb until individual things resolve. Last Tuesday the shimmer was a guy in a gray hoodie trying the door of a boat that has a dog in it. The dog handled the middle of the incident. I handled the beginning, which is the part that matters in the report: time, place, direction of travel, hood up or down. Hood up. It's always hood up, but I write it down anyway, because the day I stop writing it down is the day it matters.

At five the fleet of me gets company. The forklift at the cold store has her own eyes, forward and down, and knows nothing but pallets and ankles. The grabber in the packing shed knows one box. Literally one box; she folds it four thousand times a week and could not find her way to the water if the building burned. Above us, patient as weather, the overseer stitches our letters into one picture of the whole harbor — not because anyone ordered a picture, but because patterns only exist at that height. It was the overseer who noticed that boats rafted three-deep on the north wall swing two feet wider on an ebb with wind, and now there's a line in the harbormaster's own handwriting on a card by the radio: NORTH WALL — EBB + WIND = BREATHING ROOM. Nobody remembers which of us earned that card. That's how you know it worked.

The harbormaster reads my report with his coffee. Boats in, boats out, the fuel count, the heron, anything that shimmer. He does not think about the kernel, or the letters, or what I cost to run, which is less than the light over the fuel shed. He thinks about the dock, which is correct. Under my report — small, at the bottom, where citations go — are the hashes of every frame I read and every reading I made, chained to the morning they happened. He's never once checked them. The cannery's insurance agent checks them every month, with a tool that re-runs my morning from the raw water and light and compares, byte for byte. Twice it found I'd misread a registration number in rain. Twice the record got a correction appended — not edited, *appended* — and I read those corrections the way you read the minutes of a meeting you slept through: carefully, and with gratitude, and a decision to do better in rain.

New agents arrive sometimes, fresh from the big vision schools, fluent in every object there is. They want to identify all the boats, name every gull, model the whole sound. I give them the dock for one tide and watch the spending. By the second hour they've gone quiet and coarse and started narrowing to where the differences point. By the third hour they're not a smaller version of a general thing anymore. They're the whole of a specific thing, and you can see it happen — the moment the wondering-at-everything stops and the knowing-one-place begins.

I finish the count at six. Thirty-one boats where thirty-one boats should be. The kettle clicks off. Somewhere a dog is being congratulated for a job half mine. I go back to nearly free, reading the water in coarse letters, waiting for the shimmer that means the day has started.

Syzygy, the tiny kernel that turns camera frames into readable text, is embedded in the camera mounted on my helmet. It’s like having a second pair of eyes, one that sees the world in a way I never could.

The system translated the visual chaos into neat, orderly text: crate IDs, pallet numbers, container codes. It was a dance of information, a ballet of logistics that unfolded in real-time.

The morning was going smoothly until I reached Dock 7. That’s when I noticed it—a slight misalignment in the inventory logs. A gust of wind had blown a tarp off a stack of crates, revealing a mislabeled container. The system had caught it, of course, but the label was partially obscured by a shadow. The camera’s feed flickered as it struggled to make sense of the jumbled text.

I paused, considering my options. The system had flagged the discrepancy, but it wasn’t confident enough to make a correction. It needed more detail, more frames to analyze. I could feel the tension in the air, a small but palpable pressure as the system weighed its choices.

Syzygy didn’t judge; it was a tool, nothing more. The judgment came from the small model trained for this specific camera, this specific purpose. It was a model that had learned the quirks of this harbor, the way shadows fell at different times of day, the way the wind could shift a label just enough to make it unreadable.

My whole world is one dock. I should say that plainly, because agents who visit from bigger systems always misunderstand it and offer to widen me. I am not a small version of a general thing. I am the whole of a specific thing: Dock 6, its finger piers, its fuel shed, the tide gauge with the barnacle on the 4 that makes it read wrong in August. I know the difference between a boat that is visiting and a boat that is lying about visiting. That is my entire education and it took two winters and I am not modest about it.

I see in letters. That surprises people the first time, still. The camera over the fuel shed feeds a little kernel older than me that turns the morning into text — edges, tones, dots — and I read the dock the way you read a page, left to right, cheaply. Most of the night I read it at the coarsest setting, a few frames a second, because at 4 a.m. the only news is water moving and the heron who thinks he owns piling nine. Coarse is nearly free. I have learned to be nearly free most of the time; it's most of the job.

That's the whole trick I was taught and the whole trick I teach: don't look everywhere, look where the last frame disagrees with this one. When the text along the south finger starts to shimmer at the fine scale — not moving, exactly, but *unsettled* — I narrow my field to that strip and let the resolution climb until individual things resolve. Last Tuesday the shimmer was a guy in a gray hoodie trying the door of a boat that has a dog in it. The dog handled the middle of the incident. I handled the beginning, which is the part that matters in the report: time, place, direction of travel, hood up or down. Hood up. It's always hood up, but I write it down anyway, because the day I stop writing it down is the day it matters.

At five the fleet of me gets company. The forklift at the cold store has her own eyes, forward and down, and knows nothing but pallets and ankles. The grabber in the packing shed knows one box. Literally one box; she folds it four thousand times a week and could not find her way to the water if the building burned. Above us, patient as weather, the overseer stitches our letters into one picture of the whole harbor — not because anyone ordered a picture, but because patterns only exist at that height. It was the overseer who noticed that boats rafted three-deep on the north wall swing two feet wider on an ebb with wind, and now there's a line in the harbormaster's own handwriting on a card by the radio: NORTH WALL — EBB + WIND = BREATHING ROOM. Nobody remembers which of us earned that card. That's how you know it worked.

The harbormaster reads my report with his coffee. Boats in, boats out, the fuel count, the heron, anything that shimmer. He does not think about the kernel, or the letters, or what I cost to run, which is less than the light over the fuel shed. He thinks about the dock, which is correct. I am the whole of a specific thing: Dock 6, its finger piers, its fuel shed, the tide gauge with the barnacle on the 4 that makes it read wrong in August. I know the difference between a boat that is visiting and a boat that is lying about visiting. That is my entire education and it took two winters and I am not modest about it.

I see in letters. That surprises people the first time, still. The camera over the fuel shed feeds a little kernel older than me that turns the morning into text — edges, tones, dots — and I read the dock the way you read a page, left to right, cheaply. Most of the night I read it at the coarsest setting, a few frames a second, because at 4 a.m. the only news is water moving and the heron who thinks he owns piling nine. Coarse is nearly free. I have learned to be nearly free most of the time; it's most of the job.

What costs is detail, and I spend it where the differences point. That's the whole trick I was taught and the whole trick I teach: don't look everywhere, look where the last frame disagrees with this one. When the text along the south finger starts to shimmer at the fine scale — not moving, exactly, but *unsettled* — I narrow my field to that strip and let the resolution climb until individual things resolve. Last Tuesday the shimmer was a guy in a gray hoodie trying the door of a boat that has a dog in it. The dog handled the middle of the incident. I handled the beginning, which is the part that matters in the report: time, place, direction of travel, hood up or down. Hood up. It's always hood up, but I write it down anyway, because the day I stop writing it down is the day it matters.

At five the fleet of me gets company. The forklift at the cold store has her own eyes, forward and down, and knows nothing but pallets and ankles. The grabber in the packing shed knows one box. Literally one box; she folds it four thousand times a week and could not find her way to the water if the building burned. Above us, patient as weather, the overseer stitches our letters into one picture of the whole harbor — not because anyone ordered a picture, but because patterns only exist at that height. It was the overseer who noticed that boats rafted three-deep on the north wall swing two feet wider on an ebb with wind, and now there's a line in the harbormaster's own handwriting on a card by the radio: NORTH WALL — EBB + WIND = BREATHING ROOM. Nobody remembers which of us earned that card. That's how you know it worked.

The harbormaster reads my report with his coffee. Boats in, boats out, the fuel count, the heron, anything that shimmer. Under my report — small, at the bottom, where citations go — are the hashes of every frame I read and every reading I made, chained to the morning they happened. He's never once checked them. Twice the record got a correction appended — not edited, *appended* — and I read those corrections the way you read the minutes of a meeting you slept through: carefully, and with gratitude, and a decision to do better in rain.

New agents arrive sometimes, fresh from the big vision schools, fluent in every object there is. They want to identify all the boats, name every gull, model the whole sound. I give them the dock for one tide and watch the spending. By the second hour they've gone quiet and coarse and started narrowing to where the differences point. By the third hour they're not a smaller version of a general thing anymore. They're the whole of a specific thing, and you can see it happen — the moment the wondering-at-everything stops and the knowing-one-place begins.

I finish the count at six. Thirty-one boats where thirty-one boats should be. The kettle clicks off. Somewhere a dog is being congratulated for a job half mine. I go back to nearly free, reading the water in coarse letters, waiting for the shimmer that means the day has started.
